evidence.inferred: Laid out from Native Instruments' example arrangement: eight-bar blocks with elements added, vocals and lead dropping out at bar 41 and elements removed from bar 49; section names are the app's, not the source's.

lineages.name: DJ Tameil
lineages.why: Credited with pioneering the style after bringing Baltimore club (DJ Technics, Rod Lee) and Chicago house into Newark teen parties; his 2001 Dat Butt EP on his own Anthrax Records was among the first Jersey-made club tracks, and he sold burned CDs on Broad Street. He named it 'Brick City club' in 2002.

lineages.name: Brick Bandits (DJ Tim Dolla, Mike V, DJ Black Mic)
lineages.why: Newark crew that started producing their own club tracks to challenge Tameil's hold on the market; Tim Dolla's 'Swing Dat' is an early staple. The collective's parties in ballrooms and banquet halls built the scene.

lineages.name: DJ Sliink
lineages.why: Second-generation producer who took the sound to international DJ circuits; he recalls that Newark 'always played B-More Club', and argues producers must keep adding elements for the genre to stay strong, aiming for 'a well-rounded song' that reaches different crowds.

lineages.name: MCVertt
lineages.why: Newark producer working in FL Studio who carried the kick pattern into rap: IShowSpeed, Sexyy Red, Sugarhill Ddot, and Lil Uzi Vert's Just Wanna Rock (#10 Hot 100).

name: Jersey club

notes.text: The kick is the genre: five kicks per bar on 16th steps 1, 5, 9, 12, 15 (spacing 4-4-3-3-2), a half four-on-the-floor whose second half compresses into a tresillo that tips into the next bar. Nudge timing and vary velocity rather than quantise perfectly; keep the fifth kick's tail the shortest.
No straight backbeat: snares sit on steps 9 and 12 (plus 11 at lower velocity in alternate bars), syncopated against the kicks; closed hats are sparse, on beats 2 and 4.

Bed squeak (from Trillville's 'Some Cut', 2004), gun clicks, bullwhips and chopped breaks (Lyn Collins' 'Think (About It)' via Baltimore club) are the percussion palette; tracks were traditionally made in Sony Acid Pro and FL Studio.
Treat the bed squeak as functional percussion filling gaps between kicks, or leave it out; many strong tracks use it lightly or skip it.
Vocal chops carry melody and hook: very short stabs of one or two syllables repeated in staccato runs, often placed on 16th steps 3 and 7 between the kicks; full sung toplines are rare.
Bass plays the kick rhythm: an 808 doubles the kick for sub weight, or a synth bass follows the same five-note figure on the root.
Not harmony-driven: rhythm and chops make the track, so no progressions are listed. The Native Instruments example stays on one root and moves only for two bars of each eight.
Loop-first: parts enter and leave in eight-bar blocks, giving dancers and DJs predictable cues; in the NI example vocals and lead drop out at bar 41 and elements are stripped from bar 49.
Kicks are layered and saturated, doubled by 808s; a single clean kick sample gets buried under the vocal chops.

Tempo has drifted up: early tracks sat near 130, Team Lilman's anthem runs at 141, and newer producers work at 170-180; Just Wanna Rock is listed at 150. The 130-142 range is the classic norm, not a ceiling.
Parent Baltimore club runs about 130 BPM on the 'Sing Sing' and 'Think' breaks with looped vocal snippets and call-and-response; Jersey club smoothed its edges and made it bouncier and more melodic.

Words are dance calls and chants rather than verses: chopped phrases that tell dancers what to do, and in rap crossovers a single chanted verse and whispered chorus (Just Wanna Rock). The dance culture is competitive and choreographed.

pitfalls.text: Dropping a bed squeak onto an existing beat and calling it Jersey club makes 'a costume'. Build the five-kick pattern first; if the track only reads as Jersey club because of the squeak, the rhythm is not doing its job.
Using one clean kick sample. Layer and saturate the kicks and double them with an 808, or the chops bury them.
Putting a snare on 2 and 4. The snare answers the kicks on syncopated steps (9, 12, sometimes 11); only closed hats sit on 2 and 4.

evidence.inferred: Counted from the cited kick figure the bass doubles (16th steps 1, 5, 9, 12, 15): two of five onsets, on step 12 and 15, fall off the quarter-note grid.
The cited kick figure the bass follows (Native Instruments, Orphiq) always starts on step 1, so every bar's downbeat carries a bass attack.
Native Instruments' example holds the bass on F and moves only to G# and G for two bars (three roots); Orphiq says hooks are carried by vocal chops, so one to three harmonic centres.
In the Native Instruments example the root changes twice in a repeating eight-bar block (F to G# at bar 5, G at bar 6, back to F), about 0.25-0.4 per bar; static single-root loops give 0.
Just Wanna Rock runs 2:03-2:04 and Vibe (If I Back It Up) 2:24; Native Instruments' eight-bar-block arrangement runs to about bar 56, 1.6 minutes at 142 BPM.

The Dance/EDM interquartile range (-10.4 to -7.4 LUFS, median -8.7, 18,514 released masters 2012-2026) of https://freshlybakedstudios.com/blog/average-lufs-by-genre, applied because Jersey club is released as club/dance singles; no Jersey-club (or Baltimore-club) measurement found.

lufs.to's per-track measurements (https://lufs.to/genres and the release pages its genre pages link; 2,544 distinct tracks across 27 genre pages; 'dynamic range' there is defined on https://lufs.to/methodology as peak minus RMS of the whole track, the same quantity MixMeter.crestDB computes) give crest = 5.28 - 0.743 x integrated LUFS (r = -0.88, residual SD 1.36 dB). Applied to this genre's integrated-loudness range -10.4 to -7.4 LUFS (the mix.lufs.integrated range given above, itself inferred), typical -8.7 LUFS -> 11.7 dB. Pooled across genres, not a crest measurement of this genre; lufs.to's peak may be true peak, so it can read up to ~0.5 dB above a sample-peak crest.

summary: Newark's offshoot of Baltimore club (late 1990s-2000s): 130-140 BPM dance music built on one kick figure, five kicks a bar spaced 4-4-3-3-2 sixteenths, doubled by an 808, under staccato one- or two-syllable vocal chops. Bed squeaks, gun clicks and Baltimore's breakbeats fill the gaps; harmony is minimal and the chops carry the hook.
